Those giving motorist directions are green and white. Blue and white guide signs are the ones used for motorist services. Brown and white guide signs mark points of public recreational or cultural interest. So when you are trying to reach a town, look for green and white; when you need services, look for blue and white; and when you are heading to a place of public recreational or cultural interest, look for brown and white. They help drivers pinpoint where they are, help locate emergency incidents, and aid highway maintenance. Milepost numbering is meant to start at zero at the south and west state lines, or at the junction where a route begins. So the numbers generally grow as you travel north or east along a route. If you ever need to report a crash or a breakdown on a highway, the nearest milepost number is one of the most useful pieces of information you can give. And a question about where to find services is looking for blue and white. Lock in the three pairs: green for directions, blue for services, brown for recreation and culture. Who may pass?","fact_ids":["sec09-F12"]},"answer":{"text":"No one, in either direction.","fact_ids":["sec09-F12"]},"rationale":{"text":"Two solid yellow lines replace the broken line when passing is banned for traffic in both directions.","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-R01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reading the center of the road","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Four kinds of markings.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},{"text":"Lines that control passing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Pavement markings generally come in four types: centerline striping, edge striping, crosswalks and pavement messages. This lesson starts with the centerline, the line that separates traffic moving in opposite directions, and the patterns that tell you when you may pass. You will learn what a broken centerline means, what a solid yellow line beside it means, and what two solid yellow lines mean. Then you will see when you may cross the centerline to turn left, and how a two-way left turn lane works. These lines are some of the most important markings on any road.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Centerline colors","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Separates opposite directions.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},{"text":"Yellow on two-lane; white on multi-lane.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"The centerline separates traffic moving in opposite directions. The manual says it is painted yellow on two-lane highways and white on multi-lane highways and one-way streets. A broken centerline marks areas with no passing restriction, where you may pass when it is safe. So the first thing to read is whether the line is broken or solid. A broken line on its own is your signal that passing is allowed, but only when it is safe, which still means checking that the road ahead is clear for the whole pass. Read the line nearest your lane. Two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Solid yellow lines","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Solid on your side: no passing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01"]},{"text":"Two solid lines: no one passes.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Where passing is restricted, a solid yellow line runs beside the broken line, and if the solid line is on your side you may not pass. When passing is banned for traffic in both directions, the broken line is replaced by two solid yellow lines. So the line nearest your lane is the one that governs you. A solid yellow line on your side bans your passing, two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways, and a broken line alone allows passing when safe. Reading the line closest to you tells you what you may do. Read the line nearest your lane. Two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Left turns and turn lanes","fact_ids":["sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Cross the centerline only to turn left.","fact_ids":["sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"Two-way left turn lane: left turns only.","fact_ids":["sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"On a two-lane, two-way road where passing is banned both ways, you may cross the centerline only as part of a left turn. On a multi-lane, two-way road, the centerline may be crossed only while making a left turn. A two-way left turn lane is reserved only for vehicles turning left from either direction. So the centerline is not a barrier to every crossing; turning left across it is allowed. What it forbids, where marked, is passing. The two-way left turn lane gives drivers from both directions a place to wait for a left turn. Read the line nearest your lane.","fact_ids":["sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Which line is yours?","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-F11","sec09-F10","sec09-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Read the line nearest your lane.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-F11","sec09-F10","sec09-F12"]},{"text":"Broken alone means passing allowed.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-F11","sec09-F10","sec09-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. When a road has both a broken and a solid yellow line, drivers sometimes read the wrong one. The rule is that if the solid line is on your side, you may not pass, even though there is a broken line in the center too. Only when the broken line is alone on your side may you pass, and only when it is safe. Two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways. So always look at the line closest to your lane before deciding to pass, and never treat the broken line on the other driver's side as permission for you. Read the line nearest your lane.","fact_ids":["sec09-R01","sec09-F11","sec09-F10","sec09-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check double yellow","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two solid yellow lines: who passes?","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: the center of a two-lane road shows two solid yellow lines. Who may pass? Decide on your answer first. The answer is no one, in either direction. Two solid yellow lines replace the broken line when passing is banned for traffic in both directions. You may still cross the centerline as part of a left turn, but not to pass. Compare that with a single solid yellow line on your side, which bans only your passing, and a broken line alone, which allows passing when it is safe. Read the line nearest your lane. Two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways.","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Centerline recap","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Broken, solid on your side, double.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"Cross only to turn left.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, pavement markings come in four types: centerlines, edge lines, crosswalks and pavement messages. The centerline separates opposite directions, and the manual says it is yellow on two-lane highways and white on multi-lane highways and one-way streets. A broken line allows passing when safe, a solid yellow line on your side bans your passing, and two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways. You may cross the centerline only to turn left on two-lane and multi-lane two-way roads, and a two-way left turn lane is only for left turns from either direction.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-R01","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec09-u03","module_id":"sec09-m03","objective_ids":["sec09-u03"],"title":{"text":"White lines, crosswalks, messages","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15"]},"why_how":[{"text":"White lines tell you when you may change lanes and where you must stop for pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lee is in the right of two same-direction lanes separated by a double solid white line and wants to move left.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A double solid white line separates lanes going the same direction, and crossing it is prohibited.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18"]},"result":{"text":"Lee stays in the lane until the double line ends.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F16"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a single solid white line between lanes forbids crossing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F18"]},"correction":{"text":"A normal solid white line discourages crossing but does not forbid it; You will learn how lanes going the same direction are separated, what an edge line means, where yellow edge lines appear, and the differences between normal, wide and double solid white lines. Then you will see how crosswalks are marked and when you must stop at one, and what pavement messages painted on the road are for. These markings tell you where you may change lanes and where you must stop for people on foot. A double solid white line is never crossed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Dividers and edges","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Broken white: may cross to pass.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15"]},{"text":"Solid white edge: shoulder moves only.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two or more lanes moving the same way are separated by broken white lines, and you may cross them when passing. A solid white edge line marks the outside of the traffic lane and may be crossed only by traffic moving onto or off the shoulder. Yellow left edge lines sometimes appear on divided roads where traffic cannot pull fully off, and yellow also marks obstructions and islands, which you must pass on the right. So white lines mark lanes and edges, and yellow marks the left edge of some divided roads and anything you must keep to the right of.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Solid, wide and double","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Solid white: crossing discouraged.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18"]},{"text":"Double solid white: crossing prohibited.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"A normal solid white line separates lanes going the same direction where crossing is discouraged but not forbidden. A wide solid white line adds emphasis where crossing calls for unusual care. A double solid white line separates lanes going the same direction, and crossing it is prohibited. So the more white there is, the stronger the message: a broken white line may be crossed to pass, a single solid line discourages crossing, a wide line calls for unusual care, and a double solid white line forbids crossing altogether. A double solid white line is never crossed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Crosswalks and messages","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop for pedestrians in crosswalks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},{"text":"Messages painted in white letters.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"Solid white lines mark crosswalks at intersections and sometimes between them, and with no controlling signal a driver must stop at any crosswalk occupied by pedestrians. Pavement messages such as SCHOOL ZONE or RR CROSSING are painted in white letters on the road to warn of conditions ahead. So white lines across your lane often mean people may be walking there, and painted words on the road are warnings to read and act on. When you see a crosswalk with people in it and no signal controlling it, you must stop. A double solid white line is never crossed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Discouraged versus prohibited","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F18","sec09-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Single solid white: discouraged.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F18","sec09-F17"]},{"text":"Double solid white: prohibited.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F18","sec09-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Learners often treat every solid white line as a wall. A normal solid white line separates same-direction lanes where crossing is discouraged but not forbidden. A double solid white line is the one that prohibits crossing. A wide solid white line adds emphasis where crossing calls for unusual care. And broken white lines may be crossed when passing. So read the line carefully: one solid line means think twice, two solid lines mean do not cross. That difference is exactly what test questions about white lines tend to check.","fact_ids":["sec09-F16","sec09-F18","sec09-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check crosswalk stops","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"No signal: when must you stop?","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: with no signal at a crosswalk, when are you required to stop? Decide on your answer first. The answer is when pedestrians occupy the crosswalk. Solid white lines mark crosswalks at intersections and sometimes between them, and with no controlling signal you must stop at any crosswalk occupied by pedestrians. That means crosswalks in the middle of a block count too. Pavement messages such as SCHOOL ZONE painted in white letters may also warn you that people on foot are likely ahead. A double solid white line is never crossed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"White lines recap","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"Broken, solid, wide, double.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]},{"text":"Stop at occupied crosswalks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, broken white lines separate same-direction lanes and may be crossed to pass. Yellow left edges appear on some divided roads, and yellow-marked islands and obstructions are passed on the right. A normal solid white line discourages crossing, a wide one calls for unusual care, and a double solid white line prohibits crossing.
